newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Central Asia allies ponder Afghan dangers.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Central Asia allies ponder Afghan dangers.

text.p: Defence ministers from Russia and three of its former Soviet allies in Central Asia, alarmed by the success of the Islamic Taleban militia, discussed how to keep the Afghan war away from their borders on Tuesday.

Interfax news agency said Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov met his counterparts from Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan in the Uzbek capital Tashkent to work out joint security measures in case Taleban forces seize northern Afghanistan, bordering the Tajik and Uzbek frontiers.
With painful memories of the 1979-89 Soviet intervention in Afghanistan still fresh, Moscow is anxious to keep a lid on trouble on its sparsely populated southern flank.
"The situation on the southern frontiers of the Commonwealth (of Independent States) may get complicated soon and Russia must not turn a blind eye to what is happening there," Rodionov said.

Interfax quoted Uzbek President Islam Karimov, who had called the meeting, as saying the situation in Afghanistan could "lead to complications and uncertainty on the southern borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States".
Ex-Soviet Turkmenistan, which also has a border with Afghanistan, did not attend the Tashkent talks.

Russia, which set up the loose 12-member CIS in 1991 to replace the defunct Soviet Union, has deployed around 6,000 peacekeepers in Tajikistan, whose government is embroiled in a civil conflict with an Afghan-based Islamic opposition.

It also keeps up to 15,000 frontier guards who help patrol Tajikistan's mountain border with Afghanistan against both Islamic guerrillas and drug runners from the "Golden Crescent" narcotics producing area, which extends to Pakistan.

Russian officials have complained the Uzbek and Kyrgyz authorities have failed to help the Tajik government. The two have seemed sceptical of Moscow's warnings that the advance of Afghan Islamic fundamentalists could destabilise the region.
But that situation appears to have changed somewhat after the Taleban's gains in recent months against northern Afghan warlords, some of whom are ethnic Uzbeks.
Defence analysts in Moscow say the spectre of a major influx of refugees, arms and drugs from northern Afghanistan had alarmed the leaders of three Central Asian states at the talks.
Interfax quoted Rodionov as saying he was impressed by proposals from Karimov but gave no details of the measures.

Rodionov must fight on two fronts, encouraging his Central Asian allies for more practical measures and campaigning in Moscow to maintain a strong military presence in a region situated more than 1,000 km (600 miles) from Russia's borders.

Defenders of Russia's military presence in Tajikistan say Moscow's withdrawal of troops from Afghanistan after a bloody 10-year intervention allowed the problem of instability on the frontier simply to move to closer, into Tajikistan.

They argue that withdrawal from the region would sooner or later lead to the resurgence of militant Islamic fundamentalism close to Russia's own borders and would end in Moscow losing what was left of its influence in the region.

Russia's dominance in the Central Asia, won during the last century after decades of rivalry with British India, is once again under threat from new forces. NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana is expected to visit the region next month.
Moscow, already livid at NATO's plans to admit ex-communist states in eastern Europe, has been angered by the alliance's increasing contacts with former Soviet states to its south.
A spokesman for Kazakhastan, the biggest state in the region and a buffer between Russia and the others, said on Tuesday Solana was likely to visit the capital Almaty in late March.
Officials say 10 days of manouevres by a Kazakh-Kyrgyz-Uzbek peacekeeping battalion and a NATO paratroop battalion are scheduled for September in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.
